title: As demand for Meta AI glasses explodes, it’s harder to avoid creepy recordings
gist: As Meta pushes AI glasses toward 20-30 million units annual production by end of 2026, privacy backlash is spawning a cottage industry of Bluetooth-detector apps, while EFF warns Meta may disable the recording LED for upcoming 'super sensing' features and could reintroduce facial recognition.

insights.claim: Meta sold more than 7 million AI glasses in 2025, up from 2 million sold in the prior two years combined, and plans to produce at least 20 million glasses annually by the end of 2026, potentially as many as 30 million if demand trends continue.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: A roughly 3-4x production step-up signals Meta is betting AI glasses become a mass consumer category in 2026, with supply chain and component demand implications for camera/sensor and battery suppliers.
insights.quote: By the end of 2026, Meta expects to start producing at least 20 million glasses annually to meet demand, or perhaps as many as 30 million if the market continues trending strongly.

insights.claim: Meta paid celebrity influencer Kylie Jenner (rumored millions of dollars) to promote a Ray-Ban pair with an AI assistant that speaks in her voice, using billboard ads and video meant to normalize the glasses as fashionable rather than emphasize practical features.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Heavy celebrity-driven marketing spend indicates Meta sees social stigma ('pervert glasses') as the primary adoption barrier, not technology or price -- a marketing/PR risk to monitor given the intense public backlash it triggered.
insights.locator: The tech giant invested heavily in promoting them

insights.claim: Despite public backlash including protests and celebrity condemnation (Lorde stopped a festival performance to tell fans 'Fuck the glasses'), the Jenner marketing campaign was viewed as a success internally at Meta.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Suggests Meta is willing to absorb reputational/PR backlash as a cost of growth, implying regulatory or brand risk is being priced lower internally than privacy advocates would like.
insights.quote: Fuck the glasses. Don’t get the glasses. Not sexy.
insights.locator: Though the Jenner campaign was supposedly viewed as a success internally at Meta

themes.theme: Privacy erosion and planned feature changes

insights.claim: Meta is reportedly testing a prototype of 'super sensing' AI glasses that would use cameras and audio to capture a wearer's every moment, and executives are planning not to activate the recording LED when these super-sensing features are in use, per Financial Times sourcing.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: A move to disable the only bystander-facing safety indicator would materially increase legal/regulatory exposure and could be the trigger for state-level biometric privacy litigation or bans.
insights.quote: are planning not to activate the LED when the super-sensing features are being used
insights.locator: Hobbyists build apps to detect glasses

insights.claim: Meta quietly installed an unreleased facial recognition system on 50 million phones via its smart-glasses app in June, which was revealed by Wired and EFF, after which Meta backpedaled and deleted the system; it is unclear if or when Meta might reintroduce it.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: A near-miss deployment of facial recognition at 50-million-device scale indicates Meta has the capability built and staged, making future reintroduction (with or without notice) a live regulatory and reputational tail risk.
insights.locator: Perhaps most troublingly, Meta recently backpedaled

insights.claim: EFF staff technologist Cooper Quintin says Meta's only current bystander safeguard, the recording LED, is 'useless' because it can be easily covered with a sticker, and thinks the tech is 'disgusting' and 'unacceptable,' expecting privacy risks to compound as the glasses spread.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: A leading privacy advocacy group assessing the primary safety mechanism as ineffective strengthens the case for future regulation (e.g., biometric privacy private-right-of-action laws) targeting Meta's glasses line specifically.
insights.quote: is better than nothing, but not by much
insights.locator: For people unknowingly targeted in secret recordings

insights.claim: EFF has released a public guide urging smart-glasses users to resist facial recognition, adopt responsible recording habits, and blur strangers' faces before posting videos online, while warning that makers will likely add facial recognition unless lawmakers act.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Signals organized advocacy pressure building toward legislation granting a private right to sue over biometric privacy violations -- a policy catalyst worth tracking for compliance-cost implications on Meta and other glasses makers.
insights.locator: EFF has warned that smart glasses makers will likely be tempted

insights.claim: Meta AI glasses have been used in immigration raids (per 404 Media reporting) and to harass sex workers and retail workers, with social media showing videos ranging from pranks to bullying and harassment.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Documented misuse in law enforcement and harassment contexts raises the odds of targeted regulatory scrutiny or institutional bans beyond general privacy complaints.
insights.locator: The tech has also controversially been used in immigration raids

insights.claim: Public venues including schools, courts, restaurants, and entertainment venues have begun banning smart glasses outright, and DEF CON 2026 reportedly banned them with no exceptions, even for prescription wearers.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Institutional bans at scale create a growing patchwork of no-go zones for smart glasses, a friction point that could slow enterprise/venue adoption even as consumer sales grow.
insights.quote: be sure to pack non-violating eyewear if you need them
insights.locator: As millions of people buy into the smart glasses fad

insights.claim: EFF's Cooper Quintin argues smart glasses invert the social friction of recording: previously a phone had to be visibly pointed at someone (creating awareness and pushback), but glasses put the friction on the bystander, who must now confront the wearer to stop covert recording.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: This 'inverted friction' framework explains why smart glasses are structurally harder to socially regulate than smartphone cameras were, suggesting normalization will take longer and require different countermeasures (detector apps, bans) rather than social norms alone.
insights.quote: The friction is now on me, calling you a pervert for wearing glasses and telling you to stop recording my kids.
insights.locator: Right now, there’s less social friction

themes.theme: Rise of detector apps as a market response

insights.claim: Multiple independent developers have built and monetized Bluetooth-based smart-glasses detector apps since February 2026, including Nearby Glasses ($2.99, 100,000+ Play Store downloads), Antizuck Smart Glasses Scanner ($3, near top of iPhone charts by July), and Zuckoff (free iPhone app launched early August with an optional ~$10/year perpetual-scanning subscription).
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: A grassroots detector-app market emerging within months of backlash shows real consumer willingness to pay for privacy countermeasures -- a nascent micro-market and possible leading indicator for broader 'AI surveillance defense' consumer tech.
insights.locator: I can do something about it

insights.claim: These detector apps work only by detecting the Bluetooth signal used to pair glasses with a phone, cannot determine if the glasses are actively recording, and can be blocked by walls or bodies -- developers themselves warn of false positives and discourage confrontation.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: The technical limits of Bluetooth-based detection mean this is a partial, stopgap solution rather than a durable fix, leaving room for a more robust future product (e.g., a manufacturer-mandated recording-status broadcast standard) to displace today's hobbyist apps.
insights.quote: detecting Bluetooth LE devices might sometimes just not work as expected

insights.claim: Zuckoff's creator Pawel Szydlowski proposes that regulators mandate companies like Meta advertise a specific Bluetooth service identifier while actively recording, which would make civil-defense detector apps far more reliable.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: A concrete, low-cost regulatory intervention (mandated recording-status broadcast) could resolve much of the detection-accuracy problem without banning the underlying technology -- a specific policy ask to watch for uptake by lawmakers.
insights.locator: He told Ars he thinks the best solution

insights.claim: Szydlowski compares the trajectory of smart-glasses privacy harms to Apple AirTags, noting it took the first US states roughly three to five years to pass anti-stalking legislation after AirTags launched in 2021, and there is still no federal law targeting AirTag abuse.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Historical precedent implies a multi-year regulatory lag is likely before smart-glasses privacy laws pass, meaning the current unregulated window for Meta's glasses could persist for several years.
insights.quote: The goal of this app was just making people aware because a lot of people won’t be aware until it becomes a major problem, which was the case with AirTags, basically
